utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Case number IT-97-25-T, the Prosecutor versus Krnojelac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Cross-examined by Mr. Bakrac: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. I think that the last thing we were discussing yesterday was the population of the town of Foca and the municipality of Foca, the actual number of inhabitants.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness' microphone is not on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Just a moment, Mr. Bakrac. We better check we have the right channels.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The channel is number 7, apparently, but we can't hear anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: The interpreters can't hear on channel 7. If the booth could do something about that.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, we can't hear the Judge now either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I was merely asking the deputy to do something.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The technician is working on that.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: No, we can't hear him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I think it may be best then if we take a short adjournment whilst the technicians sort it all out. We better have it right from the word go. We'll adjourn for a few moments. --- Break taken at 9.45 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I cannot resist remarking, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, that voice distortion does cause terrible problems. However, I believe that everything is right. Yes, Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So I would kindly ask the witness to repeat once again the number of inhabitants of the municipality of Foca and the town itself.

utterances.speaker: FWS-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think that the census of 1991 showed that there was a total population of 22.000. In percentage terms, Bosniaks accounted for about 52 per cent; Serbs accounted for about 48 per cent, including 3 per cent Montenegrins; and about 2 per cent did not declare themselves in that way. All of these figures are tentative, I think.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly, sir, that means that in the area of the entire municipality of Foca, there were some 12.000 to 13.000 Muslims.

utterances.speaker: FWS-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In town itself, in terms of the total population, there was 13.000 people. But if we take the municipality as a whole, I already said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: FWS-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps I got a bit confused with these numbers. I'm not trying to say anything very emphatically. Perhaps I've got this confused with the figure of 48.000. I'm not too sure about this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say 48.000, are you speaking of the total population?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Yes. That's -- I mean, these figures go back a long way, don't they. I didn't mention them since.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, the exact number is not important. You've given me an answer. Let us now go back to the SDA rally that you spoke about. You said there were 100.000 persons present there. At that time, was there a Muslim flag, a green one, and a Croat flag with the chessboard sign; were they linked together? Was that the case there?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. That happened in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Bearing in mind the fact that the SDA rally in Foca was the first one held and attended by 100.000 persons while the entire municipality of Foca has a Muslim population of about 20.000, didn't this lead to anxiety on the part of the Serb population as well as the feeling of a lack of safety and security; and you said that it was the other way around, that the Muslim people felt unsafe and things like that?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I never said that any particular ethnic group was threatened until then, or devalued in any way. Always some reasonable, tolerant solutions were found. On the basis of subsequent events, we can draw a conclusion as to who had what in mind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, if we look at the entirety of the municipality of Foca, you will agree with me that this was one of the biggest municipalities in the former Bosnia-Herzegovina, and it has a population of 20.000 Muslims, and it brings together 100.000 persons at a rally of a national party. You as an intellectual can tell me, do you think that this is a signal, a sign for anxiety, concern, a lack of safety and security?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No way. Not a single speech or anything could have led to such an evaluation, nor should have that been a signal of that kind. Sir, if you want me to give you an answer, it is certain that other signals were more dominant for the opting of Serbs for war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that you did not attend the rally of the SDS. Do you know perhaps whether at that rally, which was held at the city stadium, whether Radovan Karadzic attended?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember that, and I don't know that really.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said to us yesterday that the policy of the SDA was to pursue a policy that suited all persons, all persons only?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. All should enjoy all rights equally. All the rights that are enjoyed by one ethnic group should be enjoyed by all other ethnic groups, national minorities, everyone else. That was the only programme that was there. After all, the then leadership of Bosnia-Herzegovina from the ranks of the Bosniaks advocated for a long time the existence of Yugoslavia; however, a Yugoslavia which would comprise both Croatia and Serbia, but not an asymmetrical Yugoslavia. Bosnia and Herzegovina has three ethnic groups, and if Bosnia-Herzegovina were to remain without one of the three dominant ethnic groups, that would certainly disrupt the balance in those terms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, you said that the Party of Democratic Action was in favour in Yugoslavia. Since you were involved in politics at that time, I cannot but ask you whether there was a plan by Cuellar, and do you remember that Radovan Karadzic signed it? It was an independent Bosnia subdivided into Cantons, and this same option was refused at the same moment by Alija Izetbegovic, and he refused to sign it?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not remember that really because I did not have enough time to deal with the Cutiliero plan that extensively in terms of all of those who were in favour of keeping a Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Sir, I'll remind you. Please pause until the translators have caught up on the question before you commence your answer. If you have no way of hearing what the interpreters are doing, perhaps you'll find the screen will help you. You will see that the typing finishes, and when the typing finishes, then you may start your answer. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters note that the witness' monitor is not on. We see that it's not on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that you do not remember, and you just corrected me that it wasn't Cuellar's plan, it was Cutiliero's plan. It seems that you remember this very well, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember the name. It's imprinted in my memory because it was repeated so many times. And I also could have slipped with the name in terms of pronouncing the name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said, sir, that the SDA made every effort to pursue a policy that would suit all people. What about the Serbs who were almost 40 per cent of the population of Bosnia-Herzegovina? Did secession suit them or not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: All right. If you just watch the screen, you'll see the typing finishes when the translation is finished. Now you may answer.

utterances.speaker: FWS-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please clarify this? In what sense are you referring to the secession of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the Serbs vote in the referendum on the secession of Bosnia-Herzegovina from Yugoslavia, yes/no?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. The Serbs voted no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Isn't that in contradiction with the programme of the Party of Democratic Action? You say that it pursued a policy that suited all the citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: FWS-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, however, until then, for months and even a year perhaps, negotiations were held already, first at the level of the former republics or, rather, the presidents of the republics, later at the level of the leadership of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Many agreements and discussions in which people from elsewhere in the world participated in the desire to help us, all these plans simply went down the drain because of the Serbs, because the Serbs would not accept anything. They simply found it hard to agree on anything. It was very difficult to reach agreement with them on anything. I shall remind you of their referendum in November 1991, when they all voted in favour of having all the Serbs living in one state.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, does that mean that I'm not saying the truth when I say that Radovan Karadzic accepted the Cutiliero plan?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I can't say whether you're saying the truth or not. Others will decide on that. However, you are putting questions which are arbitrary, in my opinion, at this point in time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, yesterday you said that the situation in Bosnia or, rather, in Foca, specifically before these conflicts broke out and before these ethnic-based parties were founded, was harmonious, that the relations between the Serbs and Muslims were more than satisfactory, and then the Serbs wanting to live in one state all together, if I can put it that way, disrupted all of these harmonious relations. Weren't the Serbs already living in one state?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. If we look at the former Yugoslavia, I don't know exactly when the Republic of Croatia voted in a referendum to separate from the rest and Slovenia did it even before that, and then came the referendum where the people of Bosnia-Herzegovina voted, to a large extent, in favour of an independent state because the Serbs did not want Croatia to remain within the framework of Yugoslavia. I don't know what period you are referring to when you say that the Serbs lived in one state. Yes. In the former Yugoslavia, yes, it was one state. And now in this newly established state, there would be a part which was that way before as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would that mean separating them from the rest of the Serb people because they already lived in one state?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would the separation of Bosnia-Herzegovina separate them from the rest of their people living in another federal unit?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. That meant that they would accept Bosnia-Herzegovina as their state with certain links that would later be determined with this other republic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that most of the people in Bosnia-Herzegovina opted for an independent Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: FWS-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you mean the Serbs when say this or only Croats and Muslims?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean Muslims, Croats, and probably some Serbs also thought differently. Sir, not all Serbs opted in that way. A large number certainly did. But may I prove this by saying that in all the big towns, from the beginning of the aggression and war in Bosnia-Herzegovina, the Serbs remained there and they live a normal life together with all the rest of us, even nowadays.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I have one more question for you in relation to the political situation, the situation before the war conflict broke out. I am actually guided by what you've said here. You said that you heard that Radovan Karadzic, in one of his speeches, threatened that one people would disappear. Am I making a mistake when I say that you are taking this out of context? Do you remember that he said that, "If there is violent secession, I'm afraid that one people will disappear"?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. You are taking things out of context. He was issuing a threat to have what the Serbs were proposing in parliament be accepted, and that is why he was as categorical as I said yesterday.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember what it was that the Serbs were proposing in parliament?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: At all levels, ever since the multi-party system was established, all accommodation of views with Serbs were ever difficult on the republican and federal levels. They were all obstructing things, obstructing them and obstructing them. I think they were just trying to gain in time so that people could get armed, so that all military formations could be deployed properly, and so that they could do what was done.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, could you please tell me, since you were a member of the Democratic Action Party, was there a Crisis Staff of that party?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. At the local level in Foca there was no Crisis Staff because that would mean automatically something was not normal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did I understand properly that there was something not normal at a higher level?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know whether there was a Crisis Staff at the republican level. You know that Mrs. Plavcic when she was forming the presidency was in charge of the people's defence in the former presidency.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the interrogators in KP Dom ask you whether there was a Crisis Staff, and what did you tell them?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they asked me, and I told them I don't know. I asked them also whether they know where their Crisis Staff is, and they didn't say anything to that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you didn't say that there was no Crisis Staff, but you said that you didn't know where it was?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this implies that it does exist. Who would be comprising this Crisis Staff when all of the Muslim population was totally disorganised, they were fleeing, they were fearing capture or getting killed and so on. So in a state of chaos like that, who would be able to form some Crisis Staff, and what would such a Crisis Staff mean? Nothing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you telling me that Muslims did not organise themselves before war broke out?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. This is a fact. Not at the level of Foca, but at the level of Bosnia and Herzegovina, because if the Muslim people had the potential or the option of defending themselves, perhaps the suffering in the war would be less and the war would not have lasted so long. Of course, if we rule out the help of Serbia and Montenegro as well, which was evident.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I didn't understand you quite properly: If the Muslims were armed the war would not last as long.

utterances.speaker: FWS-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, this is not logical since they were not armed and the Serbs had help from Yugoslavia, probably this war would be shorter?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the war would have been shorter if the forces were more or less equal, and by logic everybody then would be more cautious in attacking. How can you then justify that 250.000 people went through camps, and 200.000 Bosniaks were killed? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you quite sure about the fact that you have just stated?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, this is a rough estimate. We could be talking about a difference of 5.000 in the figure, but this is not so important.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that you told the security centre in Sarajevo in your statement that Muslim forces held Donje Polje from the 4th of April to the 16th of April, 1992, and also stated precisely from the street of Ivan Goran Kovacic to KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's true. This is a small area, while the rest of the town area and the rest of the municipality was in the hands of the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that Muslims in that period also held KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know a person called Senad Sahinpasic called Saja?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know him. I never got on well with him in any thinking in our views and in anything else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why did you disagree with him?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Simply, I had no opportunity to convince him of a different way of thinking. Time did not permit me that or the nature of my work, and so on. Also, his education and his view of things was completely different to mine. He was uneducated. It was difficult to persuade him or convince him of some logical things. Let me just mention one thing: The stage or the podium where the promotional gathering was held, for example, he sold that to another town without asking anyone. And I know that many meetings were held in order to question why -- question him why he did that on his own initiative. And there were so many irrational meetings held by the SDA which I considered irrational, and that is why at the end of 1991 I withdrew from such irrational meetings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know, and is it true, that after the war, Sahinpasic became a politician in the assembly or in the parliament of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before the aggression he was also a member of the parliament in the multiparty elections, and later as well, that is true; but it's true that he never made any public speeches.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the fact that the same gentleman stated in the public media as well as in parliament and confirmed when and how he started to arm the Muslim population of Foca?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I really don't know anything about that statement of his. I didn't hear it, and I didn't read it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, can you tell me if you know whether the house of Milorad Krnojelac -- well, you've already told us where it is exactly, but is it true that it belongs to the Donje Polje neighbourhood?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If we look at the street of Ivan Goran Kovacic up to KP Dom, I think that is all part of Donje Polje.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We will now come back to KP Dom. Would you please tell me, you mentioned here that on the 18th of April, two guards talked amongst themselves about the fact that Milorad Krnojelac was appointed as warden. Can you please tell me the names of those two guards because you mentioned that you know them?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. One of them was called Elcic, and the other -- I can't remember the name of the other one. The other one, I didn't recognise because I listened to that conversation through the door.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned a certain person called Babic. What is his ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: A Muslim from the Cohodor Mahala neighbourhood where many Bosniaks, Bosniak civilians were killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned here that after Room 12 you were transferred to Room 23. Do you remember that you told investigators from the office of the Prosecution that you were transferred to Room 21 in the statements that you gave?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible that I confused the numbers. It's a fact that this was at the top of building 2, and that's Room 23. But I don't rule out that later, while changing, while the police made me change my rooms, I perhaps spent some time in that room as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please tell me what is true, that you went to Room 23 after Room 23 [sic]?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. After Room 12 I went to Room 23.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it in the left or right wing of building 2?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you look from the yard, then it was in the right wing of building 2.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, you told us here yesterday that you lost 40 kilograms in KP Dom.

utterances.speaker: FWS-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do I need to remind you that you told the investigators from the OTP that you lost 20 kilograms in KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, but if I probably had weighed 64 kilograms and then when I was weighed in the infirmary four years later I had 44 kilos, then we know our maths. Perhaps yesterday I made a mistake in the number. So this is actually -- we're talking about 20 kilograms, and I apologise if yesterday I stated that I had lost 40 kilograms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. We've cleared that up now. You also stated that at the time that you were transferred to Kula or were supposed to be transferred to Kula that you were getting more food, one more slice of bread, but you also mentioned that the number of detainees dropped from 600 to 70.

utterances.speaker: FWS-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: To about 85.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also said that you think that bad food was given on purpose. Isn't it logical for food to improve when the numbers drop drastically and that it doesn't make sense that this is done deliberately because then they would also continue to provide bad food?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. The way this was all done, making our life more difficult, to have a certain number of people die of natural causes, die a natural death. And this was also stated for me, so that on the separation line, Serb soldiers distributed flyers where there was my name, my first name and last name, and it was stated there that I had died. My parents received this news there, 86 years old now, and also my brother heard about that. So this was the objective of those who were doing this, reduce our food and then to have a certain number of people go to their death in a different way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I don't like to have to keep on interrupting, but you really are not assisting the translators, sir. If you would watch the screen and wait for the typing to finish before you answer the question. That very long answer of yours there came in well before the translators had finished. Now, you are making it very difficult for them and for us. So please do watch the screen. Yes, Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If that is so, sir, why then when the number dropped would they improve the food, if that is the objective, as you say? That is not logical.

utterances.speaker: FWS-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't understand you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that the purpose was to starve people. That was the plan. Why did the food improve when the number of detainees dropped?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They saw that we were quite endangered. There was different thinking about this. They were left with a lot of sick people. I would want to mention -- I mentioned a sort of trick by a medical technician who went out with a police officer to all the rooms to write down what different people were ailing from, stating that these sick people would be exchanged. This was in September 1992. But they stayed. I will mention a man who was suffering from palsy, and he had to use crutches to walk. That person stayed, and he was then exchanged for a Serb fighter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, you mentioned a person called Kunovac yesterday. Can you tell me how much time passed since the time he was brought to KP Dom to the time of his death?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: From 20 to 22 days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is the person you said died from internal bleeding. You diagnosed that.

utterances.speaker: FWS-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This was an assumption based on the fact that my colleague performed a more detailed examination which indicated that this could be the cause. And also his clinical picture, the paleness of his face, of his -- the whites of his eyes, exhaustion, his inability to stand up straight also pointed to such a diagnostic assumption.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In that period of those 20 days did anybody beat him?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. While he was in the room with us he was not beaten.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yesterday you mentioned that the brothers Konjo were beaten. Can you tell us where this was done?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was done in the administrative building or in the corrections building that we mentioned many times yesterday. So on the ground floor of that building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned yesterday that on the ground floor of that building there was a room with a kind of column and also items for tying the extremities. Did you know about that room?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You spoke about Esad Hadzic and Esad Kiselica yesterday, but I don't think it was quite clear, so I would like you to explain. Esad Hadzic, what was his profession and what happened to him? And also Esad Kiselica, what was his profession and what happened to him later?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I'm glad you asked that question so we can clarify that today. Esad Hadzic worked in the automobile society. He was a driver and also a craftsman there. Esad Kiselica worked in the electrical utility company. The first person, we explained how he died early, and the second one was taken out in one of groups and killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that he was killed or is it not known what happened to him later?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I use that term "killed" because people cannot live eight years after that under the ground or in the air. You have to accept something that is objective, something that is already a fact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, for your information, the Defence here does not contest the fact that these people are no longer among the living. We're only interested in the manner and the place where this happened, and I'm asking you the following: Did you see this? Do you know where this murder was committed or not?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. I couldn't see that. I was surrounded by high walls that had barbed wire on the top, that are surrounded by minefields. This crime was carried out in a very organised way, in a very skilful way. Out of the 400 people that were taken away, nobody managed to escape, and this is -- this really confirms in the best way how organised this whole act was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said yesterday, sir, that certain persons were taken out and that since they were not heard of after that, you asked the guards what had happened to them because you hadn't heard from them. Could they actually get in contact with you from outside?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. People who would be exchanged to the front line could send messages. The police would find out that somebody had remained alive, had been exchanged, and this led to hope on our part, but it also confused us. If it was said, for example, that two persons were mentioned, then we wondered what happened to a large number of others.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you trying to tell me that anybody could have gotten in touch with you?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But how could you say, then, that you were wondering why they did not get in contact with you later?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was logical that we would be registered with the Red Cross and that messages could follow, because wasn't that necessary? Mr. Bakrac, you answer me now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, sir. I'm the one who puts questions here, and you're the one who gives answers. Sir, could you please be so kind as to say why you went to Livade via Prevrac?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was really up to the group of armed men who were taking us. And perhaps I could explain that it was risky to take us along the main road because Aladza dzamija was a target then. So as we were moving along the hillock of Prevrac, shells could be heard as they hit the Dom of the Aladza mosque.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that mean that you would pass through Muslim checkpoints or forces en route if you were to take the shortest route?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. That belonged to Livade. There was no resistance there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that mean that the route that you took was the shortest one?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. But this was planned by the army that took us there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So why did they make that kind of plan, to take a much longer route?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. Ask them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, did I understand you correctly that apart from this first incident when one of the members of the guard corps slapped you in the face and the other one hit you on the back with his baton, that you were never physically mistreated again?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was never physically mistreated again, and I said that yesterday. In this camp, in this camp. I was in Kula, though.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned a person whose name and surname I think I can mention, Dr. Aziz Torlak, was he physically mistreated or was he hurt in any way in KP Dom in Foca?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, as far as I know, and we were together often. He had a sharp discussion with Pero Elez which led to great fear on his part. He put a knife to his throat. He went to take the documents related to his car which had remained within the hospital compound, and that's how it ended.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So as far as you know, that is the only thing that happened to Dr. Aziz Torlak in Foca to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. And as we said yesterday, he was taken away on the 7th of July. After him, other prisoners from the camp in Foca were brought to Kula, and they brought me there. And they asked, "Where is Aziz Torlak," and I said that he never came here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said yesterday, sir, that you asked the guards when you heard who the warden was to ask the warden to release you from the isolation cell. How many days later did that happen?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: After four days and four nights that I spent in that cell.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct that you stated to the investigators of the OTP that the members of the guard corps were those who decided who would go to isolation cells and who would not?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, that's not what I said. I only said that I was taken to the isolation cell by the members of the guard corps. As for people who were in other cells in building 2, others decided about that: the police and those who were in contact with the police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Since you've given me this answer, I'm going to read to you now what it says that you stated to the investigators of the OTP.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Bakrac please slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, once you start to read, you do speed up. Please show down.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can we have a reference also, please, as to where he is reading from.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, sir. I just wanted to read a short sentence, and that's why I did this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: It's still being read very quickly. The interpreters would also like to know what the document is because they would like to follow it if they have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I already mentioned that it is a very simple question, and that is why I did not give any references. This is the statement made on the 20th of October, 1998, given to the investigators of the Tribunal. It is page number 2, the last line in the last paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "One guard from Uzice was deciding on who would be placed in isolation cells."

utterances.speaker: FWS-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: However, it does not say precisely there which period is being referred to. I was referring to the period when I was in Room 11, those two days.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The original document is in English, was in English, and it's a different text in the English. It says in the English version, "A guard from Uzice made the decision that I was to be put in solitary confinement." That is the original.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes, but you're suggesting, are you, that the statement was made in English? It wasn't, was it?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. It's the statement of the investigators of the Tribunal, and it was made in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: You mean this is not the witness's statement?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, it's a witness. It's the witness statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: But it was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: And the witness statement would have been made in B/C/S, translated at the time into English, and he signed the English document, but it was originally given by him in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, that's true, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: That's true. Well, you then provide a B/C/S version of it to the Defence, don't you?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Which is not the same, necessarily the same B/C/S version that the statement was given in, in the first place.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. I only want to mention --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: No, no, but I'm trying to get you to face up to the problem here. The witness gives his version in B/C/S. It's translated into English, and recorded in a document. He signs the document. You then have somebody else translate, or maybe the same person, translate the English document back into B/C/S to serve on the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: And as we have discovered in other cases, they are sometimes quite different because it's been through two processes of translation. Now, what, as I understand it, Mr. Bakrac is reading from is the third of those documents or the third version, the one which had been given to them as a B/C/S version of the English translation of what the witness originally said in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, then, he is entitled, is he not, to rely upon the document which you've given him as the true, correct B/C/S version, which may or may not be correct, but is he not entitled to rely upon it?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, yes, Your Honour, but I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, then, why are you drawing our attention to another version of it?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Because this is actually the original version of the document as it was and as it was signed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, I think we've been around this one before. You are in grave difficulty in every case when you try to say that what was said is in the document which was signed. We all know the way in which the statements were obtained. It is a faulty process, as I have said before, and you cannot, if I may say so, say that the English version is necessarily the correct one.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, your remarks about the process are right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Unfortunately. Very unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. But the only thing that I wanted to point out is the signed version of the document, the English that was signed, is slightly different from what the Defence had, and, therefore, I just wanted to mention this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, if I may say so, that will be very interesting later on, but I don't think you can criticise Mr. Bakrac for relying upon the document that was given to the Defence. That's all I'm saying. So may I suggest you raise it later.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, but I just wanted to say I didn't want to criticise Mr. Bakrac, I only wanted to give this to your attention. It was not a criticism.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Then really it is a matter for later on. You proceed, Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, how did you conclude this? Because you said in the same statement that since you were transferred from the isolation cell after four days, you thought that the authority of Mr. Krnojelac was considerable. Isn't it logical, if he had such authority, that you would be transferred from the isolation cell immediately?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He had absolute authority over everything that was happening in the camp. I believe that there is no contest with regard to that. Why he did not let me out earlier, I can make no comment about that. I mean, before I made a request myself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We are not talking about this. We are talking about the period from when you made your request until you were released, which is a four-day period. You know exactly that he was the one who said that you should be released?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The policeman came and said, "Please go out. The warden gave his permission." We asked whether we could be taken back to Room 11 where I was taken out of originally, and he said, "No. You will now be taken to Room number 12."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why didn't you say this in any one of the statements that you made to the investigators of the Tribunal, and why didn't you say this yesterday when you were testifying about these facts?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yesterday we did not discuss these facts that precisely, because we cannot go on forever like this. We tried to focus on important matters. Although, this is important, it seems to me, for you. I said what is important.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, tell me now who this policeman was, the one who told you that.

utterances.speaker: FWS-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you a few minutes ago that his name was Elcic, because right at the entrance into the building there is an area where the policeman on duty is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. A few minutes ago, to me you said that Elcic talked to someone else on the 18th, that the warden --

utterances.speaker: FWS-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but when I was released four days later, he was on duty again at that particular place of work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, sir, you said yesterday that when Nurko Nisic was injured, that you assisted him and that he was in your room. Which room was this exactly?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Room 12.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it also correct that you stated to the investigators of the OTP that Zelenovic, nicknamed Zelja, came to the KP Dom and that he was a military policeman?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. He beat the late Nurko Nisic. He repeated that several times, Nurko, when he was coming back from this torture.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, when you spoke about the guard Elcic, is this Milenko Elcic?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. You just said his name now.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would kindly ask the usher to show Prosecution exhibit -- this Prosecution exhibit which shows that Milenko Elcic assumed his duties in the KP Dom on the 23rd of April, 1992. The number is 34.

utterances.speaker: FWS-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It says Elcic, Vasilije Milenko, number 34, his date of his birth, year of his birth, 1951. This other date, the 23rd or 24th, there is no heading for this particular column, what this relates to, whether that is the date when he assumed his duties. If I said that I was released from solitary confinement on the 23rd, 24th, after four days, this really fits in. The time of his stay fits into the time when I was released from there. But that doesn't mean that this date is that precise in terms of his return to work or, rather, when he joined. The question is when this document was actually established or, rather, when these files were being kept on the guards.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, it's true that you said that on the 23rd or 24th - so four days later - you were released from the isolation cell, but you also said that on the 18th of April you heard how Elcic, with another guard, was talking about who was appointed warden, and this documentation, it was set up later according to the information of when certain guards began their work and when they finished it. So this is proof that was given to the Defence by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: FWS-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. You gave a correct answer regarding this. This document was set up later. So Mr. Elcic could have been, on the 18th or the 19th, on this job, doing these duties that we described.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Just one minute. I'm sorry, I did not see you standing up.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour, because that is not what the witness said yesterday. The witness said yesterday he came to the KP Dom on the 17th. He stayed in Room 11 for two days. Then he was in the isolation cell and there he --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: For four days.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. And he heard, when he was in the isolation cell - that means after the 19th - that the guards spoke about Mr. Krnojelac being the warden from the 18th onward. He didn't hear that on the 18th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes. I think that's right, Mr. Bakrac. But I'm wondering where this is getting us, this cross-examination. The witness has got a very clear view of it. He asked your client to be released and he was not released immediately. Now, how can he say why he was not released immediately? You're putting to him it was because your client had no power to do so. He disputes that. Now, we've been around and around and around that issue in this cross-examination. Where are we going, except in circles?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we're checking the credibility of the witness with this question. If you permit me just a minute, I will find this section that we were just talking about now. That's one thing. The other thing is that the witness is drawing conclusions from the facts that he really doesn't know. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I think you really should leave us to worry about that. We can understand that he's drawing conclusions. The questions that he is being asked invite him, in many cases, to draw conclusions. You have been asking him to draw all sorts of conclusions all morning about politics and all sorts of things, and I don't think that the witness can be blamed for expressing his conclusions to you in answer to these current questions. We can understand he's drawing conclusions. His conclusion may be right, it may be wrong. But the issue here, so far as this witness can give evidence, is that his perception was your client was the warden and had complete power. Now, you can argue with him all day and all night about that, but that's what his perception was at the time, unless you can produce some evidence to the contrary. And it's his perception is all that the Prosecution is putting him forward for. And they have put forward a number of witnesses and no doubt will put forward some other witnesses to say that their perception was the same. In the end, we have to determine whether that perception is right or wrong on the actual facts of the case. But you're not going to get very far, if I may say so, if you argue with each as to whether or not they had the means of knowledge. By all means, challenge them on it, suggest to them they really didn't know what it was. If you've got some other particular matter to put to the witness, do so, but you are trying to persuade the witness that he was wrong and that's not going to help us very much. What you've got to do is persuade us that he's wrong. I put that as a question of onus, which is wrong, but you have to suggest to us that he is wrong. You don't have to convince the witness himself that he's wrong. Do you see the distinction?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I see the difference, and I think that his understanding and his views of the factual questions posed by the Defence can help the Court. So I do not wish for the witness to draw conclusions for himself but for the Trial Chamber so that we could assess the value of these conclusions. I also think the Defence has the right to ask the witness to give conclusions to questions that are relevant for the Defence, not only for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: That is so, Mr. Bakrac, but you cannot complain when you have spent over an hour this morning asking him to draw conclusions, asking him specifically to draw conclusions about political matters and he continues to draw conclusions in relation to your following questions. That's all I'm pointing out to you. And your present cross-examination, so far as I can understand it, is more directed to persuading or attempting to persuade the witness that he's wrong. Now, all I'm saying to you is that will get us nowhere. It really won't. But if you want him to answer questions without drawing conclusions about a matter, then we will direct him not to draw conclusions but just tell him what he knew. Sometimes witnesses don't understand the distinction. It is a difficult one, even for some lawyers to understand, but we will attempt to do so. But you have, if I may say so, attempted to have it both ways in your cross-examination, so the witness is understandably in a difficult position. Well, it's two minutes two. I think we might take the break, and we will resume at 11.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I only have a couple of questions more for this witness, and I hope we will be through quite quickly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before the break we talked about the guard Elcic. Is that the guard that you asked to take you to the warden of KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I asked to be released through this guard, but I can't remember which guard took me to talk with the warden which took place a few days later.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, perhaps we didn't understand each other well enough. I didn't ask you who took you to the warden, but did you ask the guard Elcic that the warden received you?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I can't remember whether I asked him or someone else. I did ask him to be released from the isolation cell.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it true that in a statement to the office of the Prosecutor, to an investigator, of the 20th September 1998, in paragraph 6 you stated -- excuse me, paragraph 7, "I don't know whether Krnojelac had any kind of function in the former JNA. When I met him in the camp between the 18th and the 20th of April, 1992, he was decent towards me. He didn't say that he was the commander, the warden." Is it true that you stated this?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: These first two questions are correct. The third question, that he did not tell me that he was the commander, I didn't ask him, nor did I dare ask him that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I'm asking you whether you signed, read, whether you gave a statement to the investigators of the Office of the Prosecutor on the 20th Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. of October, 1998?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which part do you mean, which part of the statement?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: First of all tell me whether you did give this statement that I just mentioned.

utterances.speaker: FWS-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In paragraph 7, the last sentence, "He did not say he was the commander," does that mean that you did not state this?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have just told you that I did not ask him, nor could I ask him, nor did he give me a question to that effect -- an answer to that effect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, the answer couldn't have been clearer. He is simply saying that he was never told by your client that he was the commander, and he's repeated that here. What is the point of this?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't have any more questions like this, Your Honour. He just stated he didn't see him, and that he did not tell him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: That's right, and he said it twice now. But you've given two different dates of that statement, you've given the 20th of September and the 20th of October. Can you just tell us which one it is?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honour. This is the 20th of October, 1998.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that in this same statement that I quoted from just now you've stated in paragraph 6, the last two sentences on the same page, page 2: "I don't know whether Krnojelac became a member of the SDS before the war. I did not see him at any of the rallies of the SDS before the war"?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I did not see him at meetings of the SDS, but just the very fact. Allow me to clarify your question. The fact itself that he was appointed to a very responsible post makes it clear that he was a member of the SDS. So this is beyond dispute, because the SDS would not appoint somebody that they did not trust.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: That's a very good example of the witness drawing a conclusion, but I think that we've already got that point. He gave that evidence in chief, and I remember at the time thinking, well, that's a conclusion which may or may not be a fair one, but it's, nevertheless, a conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I didn't seek such an answer. I do not wish to interrupt the witness, but if you permit me, I can interrupt the witness. I'm only interested in whether he's stated what I have just quoted, but his conclusions, I didn't ask for that. I just wanted to know whether it was true, what I just quoted.

utterances.speaker: FWS-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I say something else relating to this question of yours, in view of the nature of the work, of my work, and that was a primary thing. The secondary thing was my activity in the party. Do you think that I was able to follow whether this or that person attended a meeting of the SDS or not? Primarily, I had no other problems regarding this. This is something that wouldn't bother me at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't know whether we need to continue with these conclusions. I have already asked my question and I have received an answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: You ask your next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that in the same statement that I'm quoting from, on page 4, paragraph 3, the third sentence, you stated: "I never saw Krnojelac there where they were holding us"?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't remember making such a statement. That cannot be so. This is unfounded if that is what it says. I stated yesterday when I saw him, on which occasions. I saw him several times moving in the prison complex with his associates and from the rooms that I was transferred to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You didn't understand me. Did you ever see him in buildings 1 and 2 where you were accommodated?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He didn't come into these buildings. A commander would not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you for this answer.

utterances.speaker: FWS-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me clarify. He had subordinates who would come and get the inmates.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, can you please tell me whether the name Muhamed Kameric means anything to you?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew that man and I knew that he disappeared, nothing more.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did he disappear? Where did he disappear from?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he disappeared from the camp, in one of those groups that were mentioned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember --

utterances.speaker: FWS-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me. Excuse me. I am -- I have mixed him up with Abdulah Kameric.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know Muhamed Kameric?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Muhamed Kameric called Meca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: FWS-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He is known by his nickname.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see him shortly before you were taken to Livade, and where did you see him?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. He was also captured by the Serbian Territorial Defence, and he was taken to the medical centre.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was his he ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bosniak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did he wear? What did he wear?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall, because often they put me into the cellar when they would talk to him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that mean you didn't see him at all?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, yes, I did see him. I saw him at one moment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was he wearing since you saw him one moment?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really cannot recall. I think he had some kind of dirty clothing on. Perhaps I should clarify this a bit more, his case. Would you like me to do that?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No thank you. I'm just going to remind you of the following, the statement that you gave to the security centre in Sarajevo: That you saw a person named Kameric, Muhamed in an olive-green camouflage uniform, with two grenades, and he was brought to the health centre and escaped from there.

utterances.speaker: FWS-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. That is not very different from the answer I gave a few minutes ago.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. So what I quoted to you now is correct, right?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is correct. And also what I said a few minutes ago. There is no meaningful difference.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct that in your statement given to the investigators of the Tribunal - oh, I beg your pardon - the OTP on the -- in 1996, that you said, on page 8, the first paragraph, the sentence starts as follows: "Kovac was commander of the Hercegovina Corps. I don't know what happened to him. I know that he originally came from the village of Mazoce and that he was an officer of the former JNA. I heard from Nezir Cengic, Fehim Cengic, and Hilmo Cengic that Kovac was a short man and strict. They spoke to him at the KP Dom sometime in April 1993. After my complaints, minor changes occurred. Nothing special, but at least it was a bit better." Is what I just read out to you correct?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your question is too long. Let's take this one thing at a time. Part of this is correct, that I did say that Mr. Kovac commanded the Herzegovina Corps which brought together in that period all the military formations from Foca to Trebinje, and that he is from that village that you mentioned, that that's how the mentioned Cengics described him. Part of your question was whether something had gotten better. I don't understand that very well. Could you reformulate your question, please?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. I'm not going to formulate any questions; I'm going to read what you stated. "They spoke to him at the KP Dom sometime in April 1993. After my complaints, some minor changes occurred. Nothing special, but at least it was a bit better."

utterances.speaker: FWS-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, this last thing, I cannot remember that. Well, it's possible, but I think that at this point in time it is insignificant. Whether it was January or February, as I said yesterday, when these people went to be exchanged, or whether it was April which you are mentioning right now, I cannot be very precise about that, either. At any rate, everything else is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me something else: Is it true that you stated that on Radio Foca you heard general mobilisation being proclaimed for all Serbs between the ages of 17 to 65, and a large number responded?

utterances.speaker: FWS-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you, sir, for giving evidence. You may now leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Is 162 the next witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Yes, it is, Your Honour. And he does not have voice distortion, so I think the microphones need to be exchanged.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: That won't take a moment to switch it all off. I see the estimate is three and a half hours in chief. Do you think we're going to finish today?

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: We hope so, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Would you take the solemn declaration, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. Sit down, please. Examined by Ms. Kuo:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: With the assistance of the usher --

utterances.speaker: FWS-162
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: -- I'd like to have this witness shown Prosecution Exhibit 404, which should be under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: You mean the document which is identified as 404 which you will then tender as an exhibit?

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We wish to have this tendered as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P404, and it will be under seal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, do you see the letters and number FWS-162?

utterances.speaker: FWS-162
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And under that, do you see your name?

utterances.speaker: FWS-162
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Under that, is that your birth date?

utterances.speaker: FWS-162
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you have been granted protective measures so that your name will not be used during the course of the trial. Instead, we will refer to you throughout by that witness number, 162. Do you understand? Yes? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: FWS-162
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, are you married?

utterances.speaker: FWS-162
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have any children?

utterances.speaker: FWS-162
utterances.text: Two.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are they -- is that a son and a daughter?

utterances.speaker: FWS-162
utterances.text: Yes, a son and a daughter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What ethnicity are you?

utterances.speaker: FWS-162
utterances.text: Muslim. Bosniak, as it's called nowadays.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see that you're a little bit nervous. Did you --

utterances.speaker: FWS-162
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. You can relax and just answer the questions, okay? Before the war, where did you live?

utterances.speaker: FWS-162
utterances.text: In Foca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And before the war, what kind of job did you have? You don't need to tell us the name of the company you worked with, but what was your -- what type of work did you do?

utterances.speaker: FWS-162
utterances.text: Manager of a company.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did the war in Foca start?

utterances.speaker: FWS-162
utterances.text: On the 8th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before that date, did you have any indication that a war might be coming?

utterances.speaker: FWS-162
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have any indication that certain parts of the population were leaving Foca?

utterances.speaker: FWS-162
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us what you saw?

utterances.speaker: FWS-162
utterances.text: Well, I simply saw that my neighbours were taking their children away. There were no children playing around the building where I lived. Also in my company, half of the women didn't come to work; they took their children away. I mean, outside Foca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there a particular ethnicity that was taking their children out, or was it a mixed group?

utterances.speaker: FWS-162
utterances.text: A mixed group, both one and the other.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you move your family out of Foca?

utterances.speaker: FWS-162
utterances.text: I did four or five days before. But I came to work, I came to work, eight kilometres away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why did you move your family out of Foca?

utterances.speaker: FWS-162
utterances.text: Well, it's simple. My son was disabled, and that's what my wife suggested, that we should get the child out. I did not have any other reason.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were you afraid of?

utterances.speaker: FWS-162
utterances.text: Well, what can I tell you? I was hoping that this war would not happen and that all of this would not happen. However, I saw that there were no children to be seen around town. Then I decided that, yeah, well, they could go to our weekend cottage for a few days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see on television or read or hear in other media about attacks?

utterances.speaker: FWS-162
utterances.text: On television. I watched it on television, and I read about it in the newspapers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you see and read?

utterances.speaker: FWS-162
utterances.text: Well, I saw, for example, when they entered Bijeljina, Arkan's men, these units, when they got into Bijeljina, when they were burning and killing and things like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that before or after the 8th of April?

utterances.speaker: FWS-162
utterances.text: Before the 8th of April.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you move your family?

utterances.speaker: FWS-162
utterances.text: Suba, eight kilometres away from Foca. That's where it is approximately.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned that you continued to come to work. Why did you do that?

utterances.speaker: FWS-162
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I had obligations in my company.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there particular obligations that you felt responsible for during this time?

utterances.speaker: FWS-162
utterances.text: Yes, these were reserves, the republican and municipal reserves, and I was responsible for them. They were in warehouses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say reserves, what kind of reserves do you mean?

utterances.speaker: FWS-162
utterances.text: Oil, sugar, flour, salt, detergent, soap. Those are reserves that practically every country has.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were they being kept in reserve for? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: FWS-162
utterances.text: In case of war. Those are reserves that have a military purpose.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I understand that your company was keeping these reserves, but who were the authorities in charge of deciding how and when these reserves would be distributed?

utterances.speaker: FWS-162
utterances.text: The Republican Directorate for Reserves and the executive council of the Municipal Assembly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you given any instructions before the war about what to do with these reserves, any instructions in case of war?

utterances.speaker: FWS-162
utterances.text: Yes, there are instructions. There are instructions that are kept secret, very secret.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you told that the war would start on April 8th of 1992?

utterances.speaker: FWS-162
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 8th of April, 1992, did you go to work?

utterances.speaker: FWS-162
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. On the 7th of April, I went there, and on the 8th, I returned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, my question is about the 8th of April, whether you went to work that morning.

utterances.speaker: FWS-162
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you go to work?

utterances.speaker: FWS-162
utterances.text: My own car.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you able to enter Foca?

utterances.speaker: FWS-162
utterances.text: No. No. I was stopped at the entrance into Foca, by the warehouses in Livade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who stopped you?

utterances.speaker: FWS-162
utterances.text: It was a military checkpoint. There were two young men in military uniforms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you told why you were being stopped?

utterances.speaker: FWS-162
utterances.text: No. They didn't say anything. They have just said, "You can't take the car into town, you can only walk."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell under whose command these soldiers were?

utterances.speaker: FWS-162
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know. I really don't know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you do?

utterances.speaker: FWS-162
utterances.text: I left my car there. The man who was with me, a neighbour who worked in the same company, he returned over there to Suba. Then I came to the house on foot. I shaved, got ready, and went to work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you say your "house," you mean the house that you lived in in Foca before you moved your family out?

utterances.speaker: FWS-162
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Yes. Yes. Yes. Yes, my apartment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you went to work, could you see what was happening in Foca at that time?

utterances.speaker: FWS-162
utterances.text: When I went through Foca, I saw there was shooting, right in front of me, practically speaking. This was falling -- what do you call this? Well, bullets. Bullets were falling. Then by the former JNA building, I saw two soldiers in uniform. I knew there was a radio transmitter there, and I thought that it was because of the radio station.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell who had taken over the radio station at that time?

utterances.speaker: FWS-162
utterances.text: I saw people in military uniforms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you see who was shooting?

utterances.speaker: FWS-162
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you able to arrive at work that morning?

utterances.speaker: FWS-162
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there other employees there?

utterances.speaker: FWS-162
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There was nobody else there at all?

utterances.speaker: FWS-162
utterances.text: Some of the people who worked for me or with me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So there were some people there but not all the employees were there; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FWS-162
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did your company employ security guards?

utterances.speaker: FWS-162
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there security guards on duty that day?

utterances.speaker: FWS-162
utterances.text: A number of them did not come.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you saw that not all the employees were at work, did you notify anyone?

utterances.speaker: FWS-162
utterances.text: I had my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you call anybody to find out what was going on?

utterances.speaker: FWS-162
utterances.text: Yes, the people who worked with me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did they tell you?

utterances.speaker: FWS-162
utterances.text: I was surprised. I said, "What's going on?" I don't know. I was a bit restless. They kept assuring me that nothing would happen, that a war would not break out. They told me that the JNA was there if anything were to happen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you do when you heard this?

utterances.speaker: FWS-162
utterances.text: We continued working.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The colleagues of yours whom you called and who reassured you that nothing was wrong, what ethnicity were they?

utterances.speaker: FWS-162
utterances.text: Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did your Muslim colleagues react differently?

utterances.speaker: FWS-162
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did you continue working that day?

utterances.speaker: FWS-162
utterances.text: Well, I worked until 2.30, I think.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened at that time?

utterances.speaker: FWS-162
utterances.text: Then I went with this colleague who was the director of the wholesale department. I went home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did somebody come and take over the firm that day?

utterances.speaker: FWS-162
utterances.text: Well, that day, around 2.00, the company was taken. There were two unknown men there. They were masked. They had stockings pulled down over their heads, their faces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were they wearing?

utterances.speaker: FWS-162
utterances.text: Military uniform, SMB, olive-green/grey.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did they take over the firm?

utterances.speaker: FWS-162
utterances.text: They entered through the wire fence, they disarmed the guards, and a few times they shot with their automatic weapons. Then from this external area, they entered the inner area. They went all the way to where the cashier's department of the company was. Then there was another porter there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened at the cashier's?

utterances.speaker: FWS-162
utterances.text: They disarmed the guard.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
